name: The Araucaria of Plaza de Calvo Sotelo

location.address: Plaza de Calvo Sotelo (Plaza de las Palomas), Alicante
location.neighbourhood: City centre, between Avenida Doctor Gadea and Avenida Federico Soto

verified_sources: https://www.alicante.es/sites/default/files/documentos/documentos/paseos-y-arboles-singulares-centro-tradicional-alicante/senderos-centro.pdf (Ayuntamiento de Alicante's own walking-route brochure, stop 8, Plaza de Calvo Sotelo: 'un olmo, un platano de sombra ... y una enorme araucaria'; the companion species fact-sheet PDF at the same URL path (senderos-centro-arboles.pdf) captions a photo 'Araucaria en Plaza Calvo Sotelo')

https://anticalicante.blogspot.com/2026/05/alicante-ayer-y-hoy-plaza-de-calvo.html (independent local-history 'then and now' blog, fetched directly 2026-09-04, no citation to the Ayuntamiento brochure or Wikipedia in this post: 'La plaza destaca tanto por su arbolado -que incluye una imponente araucaria centenaria- como por ser un nucleo de gran tradicion social y festera')
access: Free, open public plaza in the city centre (popularly called Plaza de las Palomas), no gate or opening hours
transport: TRAM Luceros stop (lines L1-L4) or Plaza de los Luceros, roughly 5-8 minutes on foot; about 350m from the Plaza Gabriel Miro fig cluster
story:
A Norfolk Island Pine is neither a pine nor from anywhere near Spain. The species grows wild on one small island in the South Pacific, about eight kilometres end to end, and nineteenth-century gardeners carried it to every warm coast they could reach because it does something no Mediterranean native does. It builds itself in flat horizontal tiers, one stacked above the next, and it holds that shape in salt wind.

Alicante's grows on Plaza de Calvo Sotelo, the square everyone here calls the Plaza de las Palomas after its pigeons. Local historians describe it as centenaria, over a hundred years old, and that is as precise as anybody has been willing to be. There is no planting record and nobody has put a tape around the trunk. If you know either figure, tell us.

The city's own walking route through the old centre stops on this square and names three trees: an elm, a plane and this one. The araucaria is the only conifer of the three and the easiest to pick out from across the plaza, a dark green spire in a place otherwise built for shade. The square is one of Alicante's social and festival grounds, which means the tree has spent its entire life standing over crowds. It is free, unfenced and open at every hour, five minutes on foot from the trams at Luceros.
